coherence.reasons: Both run the same chain: growing market, structurally negative orders, plan needs unobserved inputs, runway breached, software instead. X is tighter: each executive-summary line maps to one slide block, and slide 3 tests the founders' three claims one by one before the detail. X admits one tension: it says only software meets both conditions, yet also says core burn must fall whatever is decided. Y's question tree maps cleanly to its sections and its governing thought (software can break even on current cash) is backed by slide 28. Y has small internal slips: a finding about losses 'even before the dark store' is evidenced with the after-site-cost figure, and 'density, not store count, is the lever' sits awkwardly beside the gate saying no amount of density fixes the per-order loss.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (decline, fund software, reopen on triggers) and weigh the same three options with the same verdicts. Both reject a one-store pilot on runway grounds; X adds that scaling a pilot brings back the full plan, which covers the 'by stealth' concern. Y goes further on the investors' actual test: it models the software path to break-even in early 2029 with about $5.4M left and runway never below about two years, and states the assumptions (60% growth, flat costs) openly. X only asserts that software meets the profitability condition, though it usefully warns that flat burn hits the floor in about 18 months regardless. Y also adds a funding gate and a core-business gate, and proposes testing channel conflict with late-stage grocers. The difference is small because Y's projection rests on optimistic assumptions.

evidence.reasons: Both get every required figure right: −$6.17 median, −$1.76 best composite, −$12.57 pop-up, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, about 42% growth, and −$1.05 for the Zipcart playbook at median. I checked the secondary arithmetic in both (waterfalls, one-at-a-time misses, payback, nine-store losses, Y's software cash model) and found no errors. X uses the evidence slightly more sharply: it states the 41.5% CAGR, gives a full pop-up build-up, shows the pop-up at 900 orders a day (−$9.71) and at a standard store cost (−$17.46), a best-of-everything case (−$0.08) and the density needed (about 6,400 a day). X also makes the inference that the 14 benchmark sites already run Parcelbird software, so the claimed edge is already in the numbers. Y adds a $63 break-even basket and a 20% sensitivity table, but it says the best basket and best rider productivity came from different sites, where the pack only says this of basket and density. Y's software projection also assumes flat costs while ARR quadruples, though this is flagged. X's 'nothing in the evidence supports +$2' is slightly overstated given the Zipcart fee, and neither computes the fee case at best observed density.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while granting that the growth claim is true, and both set explicit conditions for reopening the question. X handles the hypothesis more directly: it splits it into three claims and gives a verdict on each. It rebuts 'we know how to run them better than anyone' with the facts that the benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software and that Parcelbird's own pop-up did worse than its customers. It also shows density explains only about a fifth of the plan-to-benchmark gap. Y gives the Zipcart counter-evidence more room, with a dedicated slide concluding the profit came from price, not scale, and conceding that pricing closes most of the gap. Y also flags 'nobody owns the Midwest' as untested. Neither shows that the fee would turn a best-density site positive, so both slightly under-credit the supporting evidence.

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same recommendation, same critical calculations, same option set, same treatment of the runway constraint and the Zipcart evidence. X serves the board slightly better because it confronts the founders' claims one by one, makes the point that Parcelbird's software edge is already in the loss-making benchmark, and is candid that the core business must cut burn whatever is decided. It does this with tighter logic and no unsupported pairing claim. Y's advantage is the software break-even projection and the owner-assigned gates, which speak directly to the investors' profitability objective, but that projection rests on optimistic assumptions. On balance X by a small margin.
